final_proof:
Let \(B=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) be the set of all infinite binary sequences. First, \(B\) is uncountable. Indeed, if its elements could be listed as \(b^{(0)},b^{(1)},b^{(2)},\ldots\), where \(b^{(j)}=(b^{(j)}_n)_{n\ge 0}\), define a binary sequence \(c\) by \(c_n=1-b^{(n)}_n\). Then \(c\) differs from \(b^{(n)}\) in its \(n\)-th coordinate for every \(n\), so \(c\) is absent from the purported list, a contradiction. (A finite set could also be made into such a list by repetition, so this rules out countability altogether.)

We construct an injection from \(B\) into \(\mathbb Q_p\). Write \(|\cdot|_p\) for the normalized \(p\)-adic absolute value, so \(|p|_p=p^{-1}\). For \(a=(a_n)_{n\ge0}\in B\), put
\[
s_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_np^n.
\]
If \(M>N\), then
\[
s_M(a)-s_N(a)=p^{N+1}\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}a_np^{n-(N+1)}.
\]
The second factor is an integer and hence has \(p\)-adic absolute value at most \(1\). Consequently,
\[
|s_M(a)-s_N(a)|_p\le p^{-(N+1)}.
\]
Thus \((s_N(a))_N\) is a Cauchy sequence. Since \(\mathbb Q_p\) is complete, it has a limit; define
\[
F(a)=\lim_{N\to\infty}s_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_np^n\in\mathbb Q_p.
\]
Moreover, for every \(m\), letting \(N\to\infty\) in the preceding estimate (with \(m\) in place of \(N\)) gives
\[
|F(a)-s_m(a)|_p\le p^{-(m+1)}. \tag{1}
\]

It remains to prove that \(F\) is injective. Let \(a,b\in B\) be distinct, and let \(m\) be the least index for which \(a_m\ne b_m\). Their earlier coordinates agree, and \(a_m-b_m=\pm1\), so
\[
s_m(a)-s_m(b)=(a_m-b_m)p^m,
\qquad |s_m(a)-s_m(b)|_p=p^{-m}. \tag{2}
\]
If \(F(a)=F(b)=x\), then (1) and the ultrametric triangle inequality would imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
|s_m(a)-s_m(b)|_p
&=|(s_m(a)-x)+(x-s_m(b))|_p\\
&\le \max\bigl(|s_m(a)-x|_p,|x-s_m(b)|_p\bigr)\\
&\le p^{-(m+1)},
\end{aligned}
\]
contradicting (2), since \(p^{-m}>p^{-(m+1)}\). Hence \(F(a)\ne F(b)\), and \(F\) is injective.

Therefore the uncountable set \(B\) injects into \(\mathbb Q_p\). It follows that \(\mathbb Q_p\) is uncountable. \(\square\)
